description: Interested in building something that combines science, creativity, and real-world impact. We'd love to explore ways to make complex information more accessible through interactive tools, storytelling, or visual experiences.
summary:
Rehearsing the Moon on Earth, made easy to find. Before astronauts build a base on the Moon or Mars, engineers need places on Earth to test equipment and methods. Today, those places come from a short list of famous sites, which makes it hard to search for new ones. 
Analog Atlas is a web app that works from the other end, by finding places on Earth that resemble a chosen site on the Moon or Mars. With it, users can pick a target, such as an Artemis south-pole region or Jezero crater, and the app scores every land area on Earth, in 0.25° cells, against that site’s physical fingerprint: terrain, thermal behavior, surface material, water and ice, vegetation, and buildability. The result is a heatmap on a 3D Earth globe. Each hotspot opens a site card showing what matches, where the analogy breaks down (gravity, atmosphere, radiation), and practical logistics like travel time and protected-area status. To check validity, we test whether the method ranks known analog sites highly [add result], and a novelty filter hides famous sites to surface new candidates. It combines NASA data (LRO, MOLA, MODIS albedo, VIIRS) with partner data from ESA/Copernicus (Copernicus DEM, ERA5-Land). Analog test campaigns are costly, and analog sites are poorly characterized. A transparent, reproducible way to find cheaper, more accessible sites, and to see exactly what each one cannot test, helps teams rehearse for permanent lunar and Martian bases.
details: Analog Atlas helps mission planners choose Earth sites for testing equipment and procedures intended for the Moon and Mars. It does not claim any Earth place is like the Moon or Mars. Instead, for a specific experiment, such as autonomous navigation in dry regolith, it shows which conditions an Earth site can test, which need a stated correction, and which cannot be tested on Earth at all, including gravity, atmospheric pressure, and radiation. Earth terrain comes from the ETOPO 2022 global relief model, and Earth climate and temperature inputs come from WorldClim 2.1, while planetary comparisons draw on NASA missions such as LOLA, Diviner, and MOLA. Each planetary value is graded A to D by how well it is known, and each Earth value reports its variability and measurement error separately. The intended impact is better planning for permanent lunar and Martian settlements: teams can test on Earth only where the results will transfer, and the boundary of each test is visible rather than hidden behind a single similarity score. The main limitation is that Earth values are averaged over coarse grid cells, the Earth terrain model is coarser than the planetary data, and gravity scaling is a heuristic, so results are proxies for specific tests, not replicas of planetary conditions.
